about: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures) from the Sanskrit (tools/meanings/style.md), line by line.

sh1: Three-leaved, in the form of the three guṇas, like Śiva's three eyes and his three weapons,
destroyer of the sins of three births: one bilva leaf is offered to Śiva.
sh2: With bilva leaves of three leaflets, without a hole, tender and auspicious,
I shall worship Śiva: one bilva leaf is offered to Śiva.
sh3: When Śiva, the lord of Nandī, is worshipped with an unbroken bilva leaf,
the worshippers are cleansed of all sins: one bilva leaf is offered to Śiva.
sh4: Giving even once a single śālagrāma stone to brāhmaṇas,
and the great merit of a Soma sacrifice: equal to these is one bilva leaf offered to Śiva.
sh5: Thousands of crores of elephants given, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
and the great gift of a crore of maidens in marriage: equal to these is one bilva leaf offered to Śiva.
sh6: Born from the body of Lakṣmī and dear to Mahādeva,
the bilva tree I offer: one bilva leaf is offered to Śiva.
sh7: The sight of the bilva tree and its touch destroy sin;
one bilva leaf offered to Śiva destroys the most terrible sins.
kashi: Dwelling in the holy land of Kāśī, the sight of Kālabhairava
and the sight of Mādhava at Prayāga: equal to these is one bilva leaf offered to Śiva.
sh8: To him who is Brahmā at the root, Viṣṇu in the middle
and Śiva at the top: one bilva leaf is offered to Śiva.
phala: Whoever recites this holy Bilvāṣṭaka in the presence of Śiva
is freed from all sins and reaches the world of Śiva.

sh1: The bilva leaf is one leaf of three leaflets, matched to Śiva's threes: the three guṇas (sattva, rajas and tamas), his three eyes (the sun, the moon and fire) and his three weapons. “Three births” stands for many births.
sh4: The śālagrāma is a sacred stone in which Viṣṇu is worshipped; the Soma sacrifice is one of the great Vedic sacrifices. Many read this verse and the next as saying that the offering of one bilva leaf surpasses even these.
sh5: The Vājapeya is a great Vedic sacrifice.
sh6: A Purāṇic story tells that the bilva tree was born from Lakṣmī; so it is also called śrīvṛkṣa, Lakṣmī's tree.
sh7: Aghora is also a name of Śiva; here aghorapāpa is read as “the most terrible sin”.
kashi: Kālabhairava is the form of Śiva who guards Kāśī; at Prayāga Viṣṇu is worshipped as Veṇī Mādhava. This verse stands outside the count of eight, so it has no number.
sh8: The bilva tree is held to be the three gods: Brahmā at its root, Viṣṇu in its middle and Śiva at its top.
